name: The standing evidence: Apollo you can still check
scope: A CONCEPT ladder on what Apollo left behind that anyone with the right instrument can still take a reading from TODAY. T1: on 21 July 1969 Buzz Aldrin set a suitcase-sized panel of 100 fused-silica corner-cube prisms down on the Sea of Tranquility, and observatories still fire lasers at it and catch the light coming back -- the experiment is not a record in a book, it is still RUNNING. T2: the mechanism -- a corner cube is three mirrors meeting at right angles, and a ray that enters bounces off all three and leaves EXACTLY parallel to the way it came in, so the array needs no aiming, no power and no maintenance (a bicycle reflector is the same trick). T3: how brutal the return is -- a pulse leaves Earth carrying roughly 3x10^17 photons and about ONE TO FIVE come back, so the measurement is not 'see the spot', it is counting single photons and timing them to the picosecond; Apache Point in New Mexico and the Cote d'Azur station in France do it now, and McDonald Observatory in Texas ranged the Moon from 1969 to 2013. T4: fifty years of those timings measured the Moon drifting away from Earth at 3.8 cm per year -- a tidal-friction result obtainable no other way -- and the Earth-Moon distance is now known to millimetres. T5: the targets are not all American -- the Soviet Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2 rovers carry their own smaller arrays, and Lunokhod 1's was lost for forty years until NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the rover in 2010 and stations got a return the same year. Further rungs available: the six landings brought back about 2,200 samples totalling roughly 381-382 kg, processed into 110,000 catalogued subsamples and sent to laboratories in many countries, carrying micrometeorite 'zap pits' and solar-wind-implanted gases and lacking the hydrated minerals that are everywhere in Earth rock; LRO's images from 2009 onward show the descent stages and the astronauts' footpaths.
source: Grokipedia checked FIRST per source priority but unavailable this session (grokipedia.com/page/* returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; the browser tabs were contended by parallel sibling agents and returned other agents' pages) -- the build stage MUST re-check on Grokipedia before authoring. Corroborated here against: Wikipedia 'Lunar Laser Ranging experiment' (Apollo 11/14/15 + Lunokhod 1/2 arrays; Apollo 15 array three times the size of the two earlier ones; 3x10^17 photons out and 1-5 back; 3.8 cm/yr recession; millimetre precision as of 2009; Apache Point APOLLO, Cote d'Azur, McDonald 1969-2013; Lunokhod 1 relocated by LRO in 2010); Wikipedia 'Retroreflector' (corner-cube geometry, direction vector [a,b,c] -> [-a,-b,-c]); Wikipedia 'Moon rock' (2,200 samples, 381 kg, 110,000 catalogued subsamples, Luna returned 301 g total, lunar rock lacks hydrated minerals); Wikipedia 'Apollo 11' (21.5 kg returned, EASEP); Wikipedia 'Moon landing conspiracy theories' (LRO imagery of descent stages and astronaut tracks; Soviet deep-space tracking at Yevpatoria and Ussuriisk).
framing_note: The sub-strand's flagship THEME ladder and the cleanest statement of the bank's soul: when a claim is doubted, the reply is a TEST, not an authority. VOICE RULE: present the checks POSITIVELY -- this is a standing-evidence ladder, not a conspiracy-debunking ladder. Never put a hoax claim in a stem, never let a distractor be a conspiracy talking point, never sneer. THE ACCURACY RAIL THAT MATTERS: lunar laser ranging needs a large telescope, a pulsed laser and single-photon timing -- it is NOT backyard-checkable, and no Earth telescope can resolve the flags, landers or footprints. Say 'any big observatory can check' and 'a spacecraft in lunar orbit photographs the sites'; NEVER 'you can see it with a telescope'. Second rail: confirm the corner-cube counts (Apollo 11 and 14 = 100 each, Apollo 15 = about 300) and use ~382 kg with the 381 kg variant noted, not a false-precision figure. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a 1969 experiment still returning data) and T3 (one to five photons out of 3x10^17). Distractor mine: real adjacent instruments and real coarser methods -- radar ranging (genuinely used before, far less precise), an active radio transponder (needs power, would have died), a plain flat mirror (would need aiming), the Apollo seismometers (real, and they DID stop in 1977), the Lunokhod arrays (real, but Soviet). Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'the mirrors send light straight back' before asking what a corner cube does. LANE BORDER: history owns the Space Race, the flag and 'one small step' -- science owns only the checkable leftovers and their physics.
history_overlap: history bank: Apollo 11 as Cold War triumph, the flag, 'one small step', Kennedy's deadline. This ladder must key the PHYSICAL CHECKS (photon return, corner-cube optics, sample mineralogy, LRO imagery, Lunokhod arrays) and keep the race and the politics out of every stem.

name: Sputnik's beep and the accidental invention of satellite navigation
scope: How a propaganda beep became the physics in your phone. T1: on 4 October 1957 a polished aluminium sphere 58 cm across and weighing 83.6 kg went up transmitting on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz -- frequencies chosen so that ordinary amateur radio operators anywhere on Earth could tune it in and confirm the claim for themselves; its 65-degree orbit carried it over virtually the whole inhabited world. T2: the sphere shape was itself an instrument -- a sphere presents the same drag cross-section however it tumbles, so the way its orbit decayed could be read as a measurement of the density of the upper atmosphere; the batteries died after 22 days, and the satellite burned up on 4 January 1958 after 1,440 orbits, its decay curve being the data. T3: days after launch, two physicists at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, recorded the beep out of curiosity and noticed its pitch rose on approach and fell on recession -- the same Doppler shift you hear in a passing siren -- and from that single pass they reconstructed the satellite's ENTIRE orbit. T4: in March 1958 their research director Frank McClure turned the problem inside out: if the satellite's orbit is already known, the same Doppler curve tells you where the RECEIVER is. That inversion is the birth of satellite navigation; it became the US Navy's Transit system (Transit 1B reached orbit 13 April 1960, in service 1964, full constellation 1968). T5: Transit is the direct ancestor of GPS, which retired it in 1996 -- and the core of the whole thing is free to test: stand beside a road and listen to the pitch of a passing car drop as it goes by. That drop is the measurement.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403 on direct fetch; browser tabs contended) -- re-check at build. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Sputnik 1' (4 Oct 1957 19:28:34 UTC, 83.6 kg, 58 cm, 20.005 and 40.002 MHz, easily detectable by amateur operators, 65-degree inclination, 96.20 min period, batteries 22 days, transmitter stopped 26 Oct 1957, reentry 4 Jan 1958 after 1,440 orbits, spherical shape chosen so atmospheric density could be deduced from orbital drag, Korolev's 17 Dec 1954 satellite proposal); Wikipedia 'Transit (satellite)' (Guier and Weiffenbach determined the orbit from Doppler shift of a single pass days after launch; Frank McClure, chairman of APL's Research Center, proposed the inversion in March 1958; Transit 1A failed Sept 1959, Transit 1B orbited 13 April 1960 on Thor-Ablestar, Navy service 1964, 36-satellite constellation 1968, service ended 1996 when superseded by GPS).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY-plus-INVERSION ladder: two curious men measured something nobody asked them to measure, and six months later their boss flipped it into navigation. RAIL 1 (do not merge the two steps): Guier and Weiffenbach solved for the SATELLITE's orbit; McClure's separate March-1958 move was solving for the OBSERVER's position. Crediting GPS to Guier and Weiffenbach is the error to avoid. RAIL 2: GPS does NOT work by Doppler -- it works by timing signals from four satellites; Transit did use Doppler. Say 'ancestor', never 'the same system'. RAIL 3: Sputnik carried no camera and no scientific instrument beyond a thermometer and pressure sensor telemetered through the beep -- do not inflate it. Dinner-test payoff: T3 and T5 -- the passing-car pitch drop is genuinely testable on the walk home tonight, and it is the SAME physics. Distractor mine: real adjacent navigation methods that serious people used -- sextant and chronometer celestial fixes, LORAN hyperbolic radio fixes, inertial platforms, ground radar tracking, optical Moonwatch volunteer teams (which really did track satellites). Anti-restatement: describe the SCENE (two men, a tape recorder, a rising and falling tone) and let 'Doppler shift' be the recalled answer, never a stem word. LANE BORDER: history owns the Sputnik panic, the missile gap and the founding of NASA -- science keeps the measurement.
history_overlap: history bank: Sputnik as Cold War shock, the 'Sputnik crisis', the 1958 creation of NASA/ARPA and the National Defense Education Act. This ladder keys the DOPPLER MEASUREMENT and McClure's inversion; keep NASA's founding and the political panic out of the stems.

name: Vostok 1: the engineering nobody advertised
scope: The first human spaceflight, keyed to the hardware rather than the parade. T1: when Yuri Gagarin came home on 12 April 1961 he was not inside his spacecraft -- at about 7 km up he ejected and came down under his own parachute, separately from the capsule, and the Soviet Union hid that for ten years because the international record rules of the FAI required the pilot to land WITH the craft; the admission came only in 1971. T2: the controls were LOCKED. Nobody knew whether a human could think straight in weightlessness, so Vostok 1 flew on automatic and ground command, and the code to unlock manual control -- 1-2-5 -- was sealed in an envelope aboard (engineers quietly told Gagarin the digits anyway). T3: the reentry module was a SPHERE on purpose: a sphere with its centre of mass offset toward the heat shield is passively stable, so it will right itself and reenter shield-first with no active control system at all -- the price is a steep, hard ride of roughly 8 g. T4: the flight nearly went wrong -- the equipment module failed to separate cleanly and hung on by a bundle of wires, so the capsule gyrated violently over Egypt until the wires burned through and the two parted; the whole flight lasted 108 minutes and one orbit. T5: the safety plan had a hole in it -- Vostok 1 was meant to fly low enough that if the retro-rocket failed the orbit would decay naturally inside the ten days of consumables aboard, but the launcher overperformed and put the apogee at 327 km, high enough that natural decay would have outlasted the supplies. The backup existed on paper and was voided by a rocket doing better than planned.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, especially the T3 passive-stability and T5 orbit-height claims. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Vostok 1' (launch 12 April 1961 06:07 UTC from Baikonur, 108 minutes launch-to-landing, single orbit, apogee 327 km / perigee 181 km, Gagarin ejected at 7 km and parachuted separately, USSR did not admit this until 1971 and Gagarin was made to misstate it at press conferences, equipment module remained attached by a bundle of wires causing strong gyrations over Egypt until the wires broke, sealed envelope with manual-unlock code 1-2-5, controls locked because of uncertainty about human function in weightlessness).
framing_note: Keep this ladder on the HARDWARE and the honest near-misses, not on the propaganda. Voice: the wonder is that the first human flight was flown by a passenger in a locked cockpit inside a ball designed to land itself. RAIL 1: Gagarin ejected and landed separately -- this is settled and admitted; do not soften it, and do not describe it as a failure (it was the DESIGNED landing mode for Vostok, which is exactly why the concealment was about record rules, not about a malfunction). RAIL 2: verify before authoring the T3 offset-centre-of-mass passive-stability claim and the T5 claim that the higher-than-planned apogee outran the ten days of consumables -- both are well reported but must be sourced, and the g-load figure (commonly 8-9 g) should be given as a range. RAIL 3: do not say the flight was 'fully manual' or that Gagarin 'flew' the ship. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (he landed without his spacecraft). Distractor mine: real adjacent spacecraft engineering -- ablative versus radiative heat shields, a lifting-body reentry, a Mercury-style blunt cone with an attitude-control system, a water landing (which is what Mercury actually did, and the real contrast), retro-rockets on the capsule. Anti-restatement: never let the stem mention parachutes or ejection before asking how he got down. LANE BORDER: history owns the Space Race and Gagarin as Soviet icon; science owns only the capsule engineering.
history_overlap: history bank: Gagarin as Cold War propaganda triumph, the Soviet Space Race narrative, Korolev's anonymity as 'the Chief Designer'. This ladder keys the CAPSULE ENGINEERING (designed ejection landing, locked controls, the wire-bundle separation failure, the passively stable sphere, the voided decay backup) and must not retell the race.

name: Earthrise: the photograph that was not on the flight plan
scope: How the most influential picture of Earth got taken by accident. T1: on 24 December 1968, coming round the Moon for the fourth time, the Apollo 8 crew were pointed at the lunar surface -- the Earth swinging up over the limb was not in the schedule, and William Anders had to scramble for a magazine of 70 mm colour film while the commander joked that the shot was not authorised; frame AS08-14-2383 is the result. T2: the mechanism -- the Earth 'rose' because the SPACECRAFT was rolling and changing attitude in its orbit, not because the Moon was turning under it. T3: the corrected misconception, and it is the best rung here -- for fifty years the story ran that Frank Borman took the first (black-and-white) frame before Anders found colour film. In 2018 NASA Goddard visualiser Ernie Wright reconstructed the sequence from the onboard voice transcript and the spacecraft's motion, historian Andrew Chaikin published the analysis, and Borman himself accepted the correction: Anders took all three. Even the eyewitnesses had it wrong, and the record was fixed by re-deriving the scene from data. T4: the famous version is rotated -- as shot, the lunar horizon runs vertically down the frame; the Earth-over-a-horizon composition everyone knows is an orientation NASA and the press chose afterward. T5: from a fixed spot on the near side of the Moon, Earth does NOT rise or set at all -- tidal locking pins it to nearly the same place in the sky, wobbling only a few degrees with libration -- and it hangs there about 2 degrees wide, roughly four times the width of the full Moon as we see it. Only a moving spacecraft gets an Earthrise.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, particularly the T4 frame-orientation claim. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Earthrise' (24 December 1968 at 16:39:39.3 UTC, fourth lunar orbit, catalogue number AS08-14-2383, the onboard exchange 'Oh my God! Look at that picture over there! There's the Earth coming up' with Borman's 'don't take that, it's not scheduled' and Anders asking Lovell for colour film; the article states plainly that accounts persisted for years crediting Borman with at least the black-and-white frame AS08-13-2329 but 'In fact, Anders took all three photographs', that Borman later recanted on the evidence of the transcript and Ernie Wright's NASA Goddard Scientific Visualization Studio video, and that Chaikin concludes all fourth-orbit Earth photographs were Anders's; Galen Rowell's 'most influential environmental photograph ever taken'; Whole Earth Catalog cover, Spring 1969).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder whose real payload is a CORRECTED MISCONCEPTION -- on-voice gold. RAIL (this is the one that will trip an author): Anders took ALL THREE Earthrise frames including the black-and-white one; the Borman attribution is the widespread, decades-old error, corrected in 2018. Any rung that repeats the old attribution as fact is a bank bug. Second rail: the Earth appears to rise because of the SPACECRAFT's motion and attitude -- never write that the Moon's rotation caused it. Third rail: verify the T4 orientation claim before authoring, and if it cannot be sourced cleanly, drop that rung rather than soften it. Dinner-test payoff: T5 -- a kid can check tidal locking tonight by noticing the Moon always shows the same face, and the payoff is that a Moon colonist would never see Earth rise. Distractor mine: real adjacent spaceflight photographs and real rival explanations -- the Blue Marble (Apollo 17, 1972, a genuinely different and often-confused image), the Pale Blue Dot (Voyager 1, 1990), ATS-3's 1967 full-disc image from a satellite, Lunar Orbiter 1's 1966 crescent-Earth image; and for the mechanism, lunar rotation, orbital precession, libration. Anti-restatement: never say 'the spacecraft was rolling' in a stem that asks why Earth appeared to rise. LANE BORDER: history owns the Apollo 8 Christmas broadcast and the Cold War context; geography may own Earth-as-whole imagery in its place-tour -- science owns the photograph's making and the tidal-locking mechanism.
history_overlap: history bank: Apollo 8 as the Cold War Christmas Eve broadcast and the Genesis reading; possibly Earth Day 1970 and the environmental movement. This ladder keys the PHOTOGRAPH's making, the 2018 attribution correction and the tidal-locking mechanism; leave the broadcast and the movement's politics to history.

name: Apollo 13: the failure that was built in weeks before launch
scope: An accident 330,000 km from home, and the chain of tests that reversed it. T1: with the crew sheltering in the lunar module, carbon dioxide began climbing, because the lithium-hydroxide scrubber canisters from the command module were the wrong SHAPE for the lunar module's sockets -- the fix was assembled on a workbench in Houston and read up to the crew: plastic covers torn off flight procedure manuals, a sock, a hose from a spacesuit and duct tape, and the CO2 fell. T2: the cause was set weeks earlier and on the ground -- oxygen tank 2 carried thermostatic switches built to a 1962 specification of 28 volts, while a 1965 revision put the tanks on 65-volt ground power at Kennedy; during a detanking test on 27 March 1970 the switches welded shut, the heaters ran to roughly 540 degrees C and cooked the Teflon insulation off the fan wiring. The tank flew with bare wire inside it. T3: the escape route was geometry, not thrust -- a free-return trajectory is one aimed so that lunar gravity alone bends the ship back to Earth with no further burns. Apollo 13 had deliberately been taken OFF free return to reach its landing site, which is exactly why a lunar-module descent-engine burn at 61:29:43 was needed to put it back on, followed by the PC+2 burn at 79:27 lasting 4 min 23 s to speed the return by about twelve hours. T4: the command module had to be brought back to life from a cold, dead, frozen state, on a power budget it was never designed for -- a sequence built in the simulator over hours by Ken Mattingly (the crewman grounded before launch over a rubella exposure) working with flight controller John Aaron, then read up and executed once, correctly. T5: the lunar module was rated to keep two men alive for two days and kept three alive for four; the binding constraint turned out not to be oxygen but WATER, because water was the coolant for the electronics, and the crew cut their own drinking ration to a few ounces a day. The Cortright review board that followed did the last part of the experiment: it found the 28-volt switch, published it, and redesigned the tank.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, ESPECIALLY the canister shapes and the water ration. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Apollo 13' (explosion 14 April 1970 03:08 UTC at 55:54:53 mission elapsed time, '180,000 nautical miles (210,000 mi; 330,000 km)' from Earth; thermostatic switches rated to the 1962 spec of 28 V while revised 1965 specs called for 65 V ground capability, Beech installed switches not rated for 65 V, the 27 March 1970 Countdown Demonstration Test drove heaters to about 540 C damaging Teflon wire insulation; the CO2 fix used 'plastic covers ripped from procedure manuals, duct tape, and other items'; Mattingly replaced by Swigert two days before launch over rubella exposure and later devised the cold power-up procedure with flight controller John Aaron; first DPS burn at 61:29:43.49 for 34.23 s restoring free return, PC+2 burn at 79:27:38.95 for 4 min 23 s saving twelve hours). NOT verified by fetch and flagged as build-stage checks: which module used cubical versus cylindrical LiOH canisters, Ed Smylie's leadership of the adapter team, and the drinking-water ration figure -- NASA's Apollo 13 Mission Report and the Cortright Report are the right sources.
framing_note: A DISCOVERY/failure-analysis ladder where every rung is a TEST: a bench test in Houston, a detanking test that broke the tank, an orbital-mechanics calculation, a simulator run, and finally an accident board. RAIL 1 (author must confirm before writing T1): the Command Module used SQUARE/cubical lithium-hydroxide canisters and the Lunar Module round/cylindrical ones -- the crew were in the LM and had to run the CM's spare canisters through the LM's system, which is where 'square peg in a round hole' comes from. Get the direction right or drop the rung. RAIL 2: the crew was never 'out of oxygen' -- oxygen was abundant; the crises were CO2 buildup, electrical power and water. RAIL 3: no slide-rule mythology unless documented; the trajectory work was done by ground computers with hand-checks. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a sock, a manual cover and duct tape) -- and it is genuinely reconstructable on a kitchen table as a shape-adapter puzzle. Distractor mine: real adjacent failure causes and real adjacent fixes -- a micrometeoroid strike (the crew's own first guess), a fuel-cell failure, a hatch leak, a helium tank burst disc (a real and separate Apollo 13 worry); and for the scrubber, activated charcoal, a fan, venting cabin air, the LM's own canisters. Anti-restatement: describe the SCENE (rising CO2 number, wrong-shaped box, a table of parts the crew are known to have aboard) and let the answer be recalled. LANE BORDER: history may own Apollo 13 as national drama -- science owns the failure chain, the free-return geometry and the CO2 chemistry.
history_overlap: history bank: Apollo 13 as a national drama and a Cold War-era NASA episode. This ladder keys the 28-volt-switch failure chain, the free-return geometry, the CO2 chemistry and the cold power-up; keep the public-drama framing to history.

name: Hubble's flawed mirror: when the test rig lies
scope: The most precisely made wrong answer in the history of optics. T1: Hubble reached orbit in April 1990 and sent down blurred pictures -- the primary mirror had been ground and polished to an extraordinary standard, but to the WRONG SHAPE: its outer edge was too flat by about 2.2 micrometres, roughly one four-hundred-and-fiftieth of a millimetre, and that was enough that light from the rim and light from the centre would not meet at the same point (spherical aberration). T2: the cause is the rung that matters -- the reflective null corrector, the test instrument used to tell the polishers what shape they had, had been assembled with one lens 1.3 mm out of position. The mirror passed every test because the test itself was wrong. T3: it gets worse and better at once -- two other, simpler null correctors used during fabrication DID show the aberration, and those results were set aside on the grounds that the reflective corrector was the more accurate instrument. The evidence was on the table and the reigning assumption filtered it out. T4: the investigation, chaired by Jet Propulsion Laboratory director Lew Allen, traced the misplacement to the way the corrector's spacing was set and published the finding in the open -- and because the error was now characterised EXACTLY, it could be inverted: astronomers had already begun recovering detail from the blurred images by deconvolution, un-blurring pictures using a precisely known blur. T5: the cure was optics ground with the equal and opposite error -- COSTAR's corrective mirrors for the older instruments and built-in correction inside the new Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 -- installed by spacewalking astronauts on STS-61 in December 1993, after which Hubble performed to specification. The telescope's own bad data had specified its own prescription.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, especially the exact mechanism by which the null corrector's lens ended up 1.3 mm off. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Hubble Space Telescope' (the perimeter was 'too flat by about 2200 nanometers (about 1/450 mm or 1/11000 inch)'; the reflective null corrector 'had been incorrectly assembled. (One lens was out of position by 1.3 mm (0.051 in).)'; the commission determining the origin of the error was headed by Lew Allen, director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory; spherical aberration defined as light from the edge focusing at a different point from light from the centre; Servicing Mission 1 / STS-61 in December 1993; WFPC2's relay mirrors carrying the inverse error onto its four CCDs and COSTAR placing two mirrors in the light path, one ground to correct the aberration).
framing_note: The sub-strand's epistemology flagship, and a direct structural echo of the Marshall and Semmelweis ladders: the reigning instrument/theory filtered out the true signal. RAIL 1 (the distinction the ladder exists to teach): the mirror was made with superb PRECISION and poor ACCURACY -- it was smoothly and repeatably the wrong shape. Do not let a rung imply sloppy grinding. RAIL 2: verify the T4 detail about HOW the corrector's lens got misplaced (the commonly told account involves the spacing rod being located against the wrong surface because anti-reflection coating had flaked off an end cap, letting the setup laser reflect off bare metal) before writing it -- the Allen Commission report is the source; if it cannot be pinned, keep the rung at '1.3 mm out of position' and drop the sub-cause. RAIL 3: Hubble was never useless -- it returned real science before 1993, and deconvolution is why. Dinner-test payoff: T2 -- 'the ruler was wrong, so everything measured with it was wrong' is a thing a kid can test with a mismarked ruler at the kitchen table. Distractor mine: the graveyard of real, respectable, wrong first guesses -- chromatic aberration (impossible in a mirror, and that is a teachable point), coma, astigmatism, a misaligned secondary mirror, thermal flexing of the solar arrays (which was a REAL and separate Hubble jitter problem), focus error, atmospheric seeing (impossible in orbit, also teachable). Anti-restatement: never let 'spherical aberration' or 'the test instrument was wrong' appear in a stem that asks for the cause. Teach the term 'spherical aberration' on a lower rung before testing it higher up.

name: Webb unfolds: 344 steps with no second try
scope: A telescope that had to build itself a million miles from any repairman. T1: Webb's 6.5-metre mirror is too wide for any rocket fairing, so it flew FOLDED -- eighteen gold-coated beryllium hexagons with the outer wings hinged back, launched on 25 December 2021, and unfolded over about two weeks on the way out. T2: engineers counted 344 single-point failures in the deployment -- 344 steps with no backup, no redundancy and no rescue, because Webb's destination is the Sun-Earth L2 point about 1.5 million km away, roughly four times farther than the Moon and far beyond any servicing mission. Every one of them worked. T3: the sunshield mechanism, which is not insulation -- five kite-shaped membrane layers, about 21 by 14 metres, each thinner than a human hair and separated by vacuum gaps, so each layer absorbs heat and radiates most of it sideways out of the gap; the temperature falls in five steps from roughly 110 degrees C on the sun side to about minus 235 degrees C on the telescope side. T4: after unfolding, Webb had to be TAUGHT its own shape -- it pointed at a single star, HD 84406, and saw EIGHTEEN separate images of it, one per segment; over about three months tiny actuators nudged each segment in steps of roughly 10 nanometres until all eighteen images stacked into one. T5: the price of the design is honest and permanent -- L2 was chosen because Sun, Earth and Moon all stay in the same direction so a single shield blocks all three, but that same shield means Webb can only ever look at part of the sky at any moment, and unlike Hubble, which astronauts repaired five times, Webb can never be serviced. The first science images were released in July 2022.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'James Webb Space Telescope' ('344 potential single-point failures'; 18 hexagonal gold-coated beryllium segments totalling 6.5 m; five sunshield layers each about 0.1 mm thick with deployed dimensions 14.162 m x 21.197 m; launch 25 December 2021 12:20 UTC on Ariane 5 from French Guiana; L2 approximately 1,500,000 km beyond Earth's orbit; first images released 11 July 2022; the 2018 sunshield-membrane tears during ground testing). NASA 'Webb FAQ' (science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/faqs-full/: about a month to travel to L2, roughly 1 million miles / 1.5 million km, telescope and instruments below 50 K, NIR instruments about 39 K, MIRI at 7 K, deployment was human-commanded with planned pauses rather than fully automatic). Flagged for build-stage verification: the widely reported 178 release mechanisms, the 383 K hot-side / 36 K cold-side sunshield figures, the 10-nanometre actuator step, HD 84406 as the alignment target, and the roughly 39 percent instantaneous sky coverage.
framing_note: An ENGINEERING-as-experiment ladder: the wonder is the count (344) and the teaching rung is the sunshield's radiative staircase. RAIL 1: 'zero misses' is the accurate claim about deployment, but do NOT imply Webb has had no problems -- a micrometeoroid struck segment C3 in May 2022 and left permanent damage; if a rung wants a caveat, that is the honest one. RAIL 2: verify the numeric details listed in source as unconfirmed (178 mechanisms, exact shield temperatures, actuator step size, HD 84406, sky-coverage fraction) before any of them becomes an answer; do not invent precision. RAIL 3: Webb is an INFRARED telescope, not 'a bigger Hubble' -- the cold is the whole point, because a warm telescope glows in the band it is trying to observe. That is itself a good rung. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- the five-layer radiative staircase can be felt with two sheets of foil and a lamp, and T4, because 'eighteen pictures of one star' is a scene a kid can hold. Distractor mine: real adjacent engineering choices -- an inflatable mirror, a single monolithic mirror (what Hubble has, and the reason Webb could not), active cooling by cryocooler (real, and MIRI actually uses one), a shield of thick insulation, deployment by astronauts, a low Earth orbit. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say the shield 'radiates heat between layers' before asking how it works.

name: The Voyagers: a 175-year window and a signal still coming home
scope: The mission that had to launch in 1977 or wait two centuries. T1: two spacecraft launched in 1977 are still transmitting -- Voyager 1 is now more than 25 billion km out, and its signal, radiated at a few tens of watts, takes over 23 hours to reach Earth each way. T2: the reason for 1977 -- in the mid-1960s JPL engineer Gary Flandro worked out that Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune would line up so a single craft could be flung from one to the next, an arrangement that recurs only about every 175 years. Miss the window and the next one is around the middle of the 2150s. T3: the mechanism of a gravity assist, and the counter-intuitive part -- the spacecraft does not get energy from nowhere; it steals a sliver of the PLANET's orbital momentum. Voyager gained tens of thousands of km/h and Jupiter was slowed by an amount too small to measure, because momentum is conserved and Jupiter is 10^24 times heavier. T4: how we know Voyager 1 actually left the Sun's bubble -- there was no signpost, and its plasma detector had failed back in 1980. Instead, an outburst from the Sun reached the surrounding gas and made it ring; Voyager's plasma wave instrument recorded those oscillations starting 9 April 2013, and Don Gurnett's team read an eighty-fold jump in electron density off the ringing frequency, which back-dated the heliopause crossing to 25 August 2012 at 121 astronomical units. The answer came from a broken instrument's healthy neighbour. T5: bolted to each craft is a gold-plated copper record carrying 116 images, spoken greetings in 55 languages, about ninety minutes of music, birdsong and whale song, and an hour of Ann Druyan's brainwaves compressed to a minute -- and electroplated on the cover, a spot of ultra-pure uranium-238, half-life 4.468 billion years, so that a finder can date the record by measuring how much has decayed. It is a clock designed to be read by someone who shares no language with us. Further rungs: Voyager 2 launched FIRST, on 20 August 1977, sixteen days before Voyager 1, which then overtook it on a faster path; Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft ever to have visited Uranus and Neptune; the Pale Blue Dot image was taken on 14 February 1990 from about 6 billion km; the radioisotope generators started at about 470 watts and fade as plutonium-238 decays with an 87.7-year half-life, which is why instruments are being switched off one by one.

Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Voyager 1' (launch 5 September 1977 12:56:01 UTC from LC-41; crossed the heliopause at 121 AU entering interstellar space on 25 August 2012, confirmed by an eighty-fold increase in electron density inferred from plasma oscillation frequency observed beginning 9 April 2013, with Don Gurnett as key researcher; as of August 2026 at 172.59 AU = 25.8 billion km with one-way signal time over 23 hours; RTGs about 470 W at launch, plutonium-238 half-life 87.7 years, operations projected to end 2027-2036; Pale Blue Dot 14 February 1990 from 6 billion km); Wikipedia 'Voyager program' (the Grand Tour alignment recurs 'once every 175 years'; Gary Flandro at JPL conceptualised it in 1964; gravity assist demonstrated by Mariner 10; Carl Sagan chaired the Golden Record committee; Voyager 2 the only craft to visit all four outer planets); Wikipedia 'Voyager Golden Record' (116 images including one calibration frame, spoken greetings in 55 ancient and modern languages, roughly 90 minutes of music, natural sounds including surf, wind, thunder, birds and whales, Ann Druyan's hour of brainwaves compressed to a minute, ultra-pure uranium-238 electroplated on the aluminium cover with a 4.468-billion-year half-life so a finder can date the record).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder with a genuine MECHANISM spine (gravity assist) and a beautiful how-we-know rung (T4). RAIL 1: the Grand Tour alignment is reported as roughly every 175 years (some sources say 176) and Flandro's work is dated 1964 in some sources and 1965 in others -- give the interval as 'about every 175 years' and either source the year precisely or leave it out; a bare-date question would be banned rote anyway. RAIL 2: T4 must be told correctly -- Voyager 1's plasma SCIENCE instrument had failed, so the density was inferred from the PLASMA WAVE instrument measuring oscillation frequency; do not write that Voyager 'measured the density directly' or that it 'crossed a line'. RAIL 3: interstellar space is not outside the Solar System -- Voyager 1 has left the heliosphere but is nowhere near leaving the Sun's gravity or the Oort cloud. This misconception is extremely common and correcting it is an on-voice rung. RAIL 4: the Golden Record cover's uranium is a CLOCK, not a power source. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (gravity assist as momentum theft -- testable in spirit by bouncing a ball off an advancing wall) and T5 (the uranium clock). Distractor mine: real adjacent propulsion and real rival explanations -- ion drives, solar sails, the Oberth effect, aerobraking, the slingshot 'getting free energy' (the misconception itself, which the mechanism rung refutes); for T4, a magnetic-field direction change (which was genuinely EXPECTED to mark the boundary and did NOT behave as predicted -- a superb distractor because it was the mainstream prediction), a drop in cosmic-ray count, a temperature change. Anti-restatement: never let a stem mention plasma density before asking how the crossing was confirmed.
history_overlap: history bank: the Golden Record may appear as a 1970s cultural artifact and Carl Sagan as a public figure. If so, science must key the record's ENCODING and the uranium-238 dating clock, not its cultural reception or Sagan's celebrity.

name: Opportunity and Ingenuity: the missions that outlived their own arithmetic
scope: Two Mars machines whose engineers were wrong in the lucky direction, and honest about it. T1: Opportunity was designed for 90 sols. It worked for 5,111 sols -- fourteen years and 138 days -- and drove 45.16 km, a marathon on another planet, after landing on 25 January 2004. T2: WHY it lasted is the rung that matters, and it is not heroism -- the mission's lifetime estimate assumed dust would steadily smother the solar panels. What nobody had modelled were the wind gusts that periodically swept the panels clean and restored the power; the margin came from a phenomenon the planners did not know was there. T3: what it actually found -- Opportunity bounced to a stop inside a small crater with layered bedrock exposed at wheel height, and in that outcrop it found tiny grey haematite spheres nicknamed blueberries, together with sulfate salts. On Earth those minerals form in standing, acidic water. The rover was a field geologist and its verdict was that this ground had once been soaked. T4: the ending was the same weather that had kept it alive -- a planet-encircling dust storm in June 2018 blacked out the sky, the last signal came on 10 June 2018, and the mission was declared over on 13 February 2019. T5: Ingenuity answered a different objection -- that a helicopter cannot fly on Mars, where the air is about one per cent as dense as Earth's at sea level. The answer was a 1.8 kg machine with two counter-rotating 1.21-metre rotors turning at around 2,400 rpm, roughly eight times a terrestrial helicopter's rotor speed, helped by Martian gravity being 38 per cent of Earth's. It was funded for five flights in thirty sols; it flew 72 times over nearly three years, covering 17.2 km and 2 hours 8 minutes in the air, until on 18 January 2024 it came down over bland, featureless ground its navigation camera could not read, and snapped a rotor blade. Bolted underneath it was a scrap of wing cloth from the 1903 Wright Flyer.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, especially the 'blueberries' nickname and the Eagle crater landing. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Opportunity (rover)' (landed 25 January 2004; planned 90 sols / 92.5 Earth days; operated 5,111 sols = 14 years 138 days; 45.16 km driven; last contact 10 June 2018, end declared 13 February 2019, cause the 2018 planet-encircling dust storm obscuring the solar panels; landed in Eagle crater at Meridiani Planum; found haematite and Martian spherules and substantial evidence of past water; dust-clearing winds had recovered the panels previously); Wikipedia 'Ingenuity (helicopter)' (first flight 19 April 2021 07:34 UTC; rotors 2400-2700 rpm, 1.21 m diameter; mass 1.8 kg; Martian atmosphere about 1/100 of Earth's at sea level; originally five flights in a 30-sol demonstration, 72 flights actually flown; mission ended 18 January 2024 when a rotor blade broke and other blade tips were damaged during a landing after navigation failure over featureless terrain; cumulative 2 h 8 min 48 s and 17.242 km horizontal; a piece of wing cloth from the 1903 Wright Flyer attached beneath the solar panel).
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder whose spine is intellectual honesty about MARGINS: both machines beat their design life for reasons the designers had not predicted, and the bank should say that plainly rather than tell a heroism story. RAIL 1: the cleaning events are the honest cause of Opportunity's longevity -- do not attribute it to 'good engineering' alone, and do not claim engineers designed for them. RAIL 2: verify the 'blueberries' nickname and the Eagle crater landing framing before authoring; Wikipedia uses 'Martian spherules' and does not use 'hole in one', so source the colloquial terms from NASA/JPL material or drop them. RAIL 3: the reason flight on Mars is hard is the LIFT EQUATION (lift scales with air density and with the square of blade speed), and low Martian gravity partly rescues it -- do not write 'there is no air on Mars'. RAIL 4: Ingenuity's rotors are coaxial and counter-rotating, which is why it needs no tail rotor -- a good mechanism rung, not decoration. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (2,400 rpm and a Wright Flyer scrap) and T2 (the wind saved it). Distractor mine: real adjacent Mars hardware and real rival explanations -- Spirit (the twin, which got stuck in soft soil in 2009 and is constantly confused with Opportunity), Sojourner, Curiosity and Perseverance's nuclear RTG power (the real alternative to solar), a bigger battery, a dust brush (a proposed and rejected fix); for the water evidence, wind-blown dust, volcanic ash, meteoritic material, frost. Anti-restatement: never let a stem mention wind or dust-clearing before asking why Opportunity survived. LANE BORDER: geography tours Mars as a place -- science owns the rover's EVIDENCE CHAIN and the rotor physics.
history_overlap: geography bank may tour Martian landforms and Meridiani Planum as a place. This ladder keys the rover's evidence chain (haematite spherules and sulfates implying standing acidic water), the unmodelled cleaning events, and the one-per-cent-atmosphere rotor physics -- not a place-tour of Mars.

name: DART: the first time humans deliberately moved a world
scope: Planetary defence tested rather than argued about. T1: on 26 September 2022 a 500 kg spacecraft flew itself into a 160-metre asteroid moonlet at 6.6 km per second -- about 22,500 km/h -- streaming a picture a second until the rock filled the frame and the signal stopped. T2: the target was chosen to make the answer MEASURABLE, which is the experimental-design rung -- nudging a lone asteroid's orbit around the Sun would produce a change too small to detect, but Dimorphos orbits its parent Didymos in just under twelve hours, and Earth telescopes can time the regular dip in brightness as it passes in front of and behind its parent to within seconds. The experiment was built around what could be checked. T3: the result -- the orbit shortened by about 32 to 33 minutes. Mission success had been defined in advance as any change of at least 73 seconds. The effect was more than twenty times the bar. T4: the mechanism of the overshoot -- most of the push did not come from the spacecraft. The impact blasted out a plume of rock that streamed away like exhaust from a rocket nozzle, and that recoil multiplied the momentum transfer by a factor of roughly 3.6 (the beta factor), so the debris shoved harder than the spacecraft did. T5: two honest caveats. First, Didymos and Dimorphos were never on a course to hit Earth, and DART did not make them one -- the pair was chosen because it was safe and observable. Second, beta depends on what the asteroid is MADE of, which is still not well known, so the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft launched in October 2024 to arrive in 2026, measure the crater and weigh Dimorphos, and turn a demonstration into a calibrated number. Further rung: DART had to find its own target -- Dimorphos was too small to resolve until the last hour, so the SMART Nav software picked it out of the pair and steered without help, because the radio round trip was far too long for anyone on Earth to fly it.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build, especially the pre-impact orbital period. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Double Asteroid Redirection Test' (impact 26 September 2022 at 23:14 UTC; Dimorphos about 160 m across, Didymos about 780 m; DART mass at impact 500 kg; impact speed 6.6 km/s = 22,530 km/h; orbital period change of 33 +/- 1 minutes against a defined success threshold of 73 seconds; momentum enhancement factor beta of 3.6; LICIACube separated 11 September 2022, fifteen days before impact; ESA's Hera launched October 2024 to arrive 2026). Flagged for build-stage verification: the pre-impact period is given in that article as 11 h 52 min while NASA's release commonly cites about 11 h 55 min -- author as 'just under twelve hours' unless pinned; NASA's first announcement was a 32-minute change later refined to 33 +/- 1, so quote a range; and confirm the SMART Nav terminal-guidance detail and the DRACO one-image-per-second downlink.
framing_note: The purest 'tested, not theorised' ladder in the sub-strand, and its best rung is T2 -- experimental DESIGN, choosing a target because the result could be measured. RAIL 1 (non-negotiable): DART changed Dimorphos's orbit AROUND DIDYMOS, not the pair's orbit around the Sun, and neither body threatened Earth before or after. Any stem implying humanity deflected an incoming asteroid is a bank bug. RAIL 2: give the period change as 'about 32-33 minutes' (NASA announced 32, refined analysis 33 +/- 1) and the success bar as 73 seconds -- both figures are the wonder, so get them right. RAIL 3: teach 'momentum' before testing beta, and describe beta as 'the debris pushed about 3.6 times harder than the spacecraft alone' rather than using the symbol. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (73 seconds asked for, half an hour delivered) -- and the eclipse-timing method in T2 is genuinely amateur-checkable, since backyard telescopes contributed light curves. Distractor mine: real adjacent deflection proposals that serious people have published -- a gravity tractor, a nuclear standoff burst, painting the asteroid white to use sunlight pressure (the Yarkovsky effect, real), an ion-beam shepherd, laser ablation; and for the measurement, radar ranging, a transponder, direct imaging. Anti-restatement: never let a stem mention the ejecta plume before asking why the push exceeded the spacecraft's own momentum.

name: The sky does fall: Tunguska, Chelyabinsk and the airburst
scope: Two Russian mornings a century apart, and how the second one got measured. T1: on 15 February 2013 a rock about 18-20 metres across and some 9,000 tonnes entered the air over Chelyabinsk at roughly 19 km per second and blew apart with the energy of about 400-500 kilotons of TNT, brightest around 23 km up. Nearly 1,500 people needed medical treatment and almost all of them were cut by flying window glass -- because the flash came first in silence, people crowded to their windows to look, and the shock wave took about two minutes to arrive. Light outruns sound, and that is why they were hurt. T2: nobody saw it coming -- it approached from the direction of the Sun, invisible to survey telescopes -- and it became the best-measured impact in history by accident, because Russian drivers keep dashboard cameras running. Scientists triangulated dozens of amateur videos to reconstruct the object's speed, its path and its orbit before it hit. Ordinary instruments did the science. T3: it was measured a second, independent way -- the infrasound network built to listen for clandestine nuclear tests picked the airburst up on some twenty stations around the world, giving an energy estimate that owed nothing to any video. Two utterly different instruments, one answer. T4: the mechanism, which is why there is usually no crater -- a stony body moving that fast meets air pressure far greater than its own strength, so it flattens, fragments and dumps its energy into a small volume of air in a fraction of a second. It is an explosion in the sky, not an impact in the ground. T5: Tunguska, 30 June 1908, is the same mechanism at a far larger scale -- about 2,150 square kilometres of Siberian forest flattened, and when Leonid Kulik finally reached the site in 1927 expecting an iron crater he found none: at the centre the trees were still STANDING, scorched and stripped of branches, while further out they lay knocked flat pointing away. The missing crater was the evidence. And the honest open part: published energy estimates still range from roughly 3 to 50 megatons, no fragment of the impactor has ever been confirmed, and whether it was a stony asteroid or a comet is still argued -- one 2001 orbital study put about 83 per cent odds on an asteroidal path. No one yet knows for certain.
source: Grokipedia checked first but unavailable this session (403; tabs contended) -- re-check at build. Corroborated: Wikipedia 'Chelyabinsk meteor' (15 February 2013 at 09:20:28 local; approximately 18 m and 9,100 tonnes; entry speed about 19.2 km/s; energy 400-500 kilotons of TNT with higher outlier estimates; airburst about 30 km with peak brightness at 23.3 km; 1,491 people injured seriously enough to seek treatment, damage primarily from broken window glass blown in when the shock wave arrived; about 7,200 buildings in six cities damaged; the object approached undetected; infrasound from the explosion detected by 20 monitoring stations; a 654 kg fragment recovered from Lake Chebarkul on 16 October 2013); Wikipedia 'Tunguska event' (30 June 1908 at 07:17 local; 2,150 km2 of forest flattened; the widely repeated 80-million-trees figure explicitly flagged in the article as based on a preliminary guess; energy estimates 3-50 megatons with recent work at 3-5 Mt and a 2019 paper at 20-30 Mt; airburst 5-10 km altitude; Leonid Kulik's 1927 expedition expected a crater and found instead a zone about 8 km across where trees were scorched and stripped of branches but still standing upright, with trees further out knocked down away from the centre; a 2001 study giving 83 per cent probability of an asteroidal path versus 17 per cent cometary; no crater and no confirmed fragments).
framing_note: A MECHANISM-plus-MYSTERY theme ladder, and the sub-strand's best 'measurement got democratised' story. RAIL 1 (Wikipedia flags this explicitly and the bank must not repeat the error): the famous '80 million trees' at Tunguska is a PRELIMINARY GUESS, not a count -- use the 2,150 km2 flattened-forest figure, which is measured. RAIL 2: T5 is a genuine MYSTERY rung -- say 'no one yet knows' proudly about the impactor's nature and the exact energy, and make absolutely sure no distractor is secretly the truth; do not let a rung imply the comet-versus-asteroid question is settled. RAIL 3: Chelyabinsk was an AIRBURST -- the 654 kg Chebarkul fragment is a surviving piece, not the intact body; do not describe it as 'the meteorite that hit'. RAIL 4: give Chelyabinsk energy as 400-500 kt and injuries as roughly 1,500 seeking treatment, with glass as the dominant cause. Dinner-test payoff: T1 -- the two-minute gap between flash and blast is exactly the thunder-counting experiment a kid can run in the next storm, and the injury pattern makes it unforgettable and useful. Distractor mine: real adjacent explanations that scientists actually proposed -- a comet nucleus, a small black hole, antimatter, a natural gas eruption (all genuinely published for Tunguska), and for the no-crater puzzle, a buried impactor, a lake as the crater (Lake Cheko has been seriously proposed and seriously disputed), complete vaporisation. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'it exploded in the air' before asking why Kulik found no crater. LANE BORDER: geography owns Siberia and Tunguska as a place and owns impact craters as landforms -- science owns the airburst mechanism, the absent-crater inference, and the infrasound and dashcam measurements.
history_overlap: geography bank: Tunguska/Siberia as a place and impact craters as landforms may already be toured there. This ladder keys the AIRBURST MECHANISM, Kulik's absent crater as evidence, and the dashcam plus infrasound measurement of Chelyabinsk -- not the geography of the region.
